facts.label: F3
facts.text: [F3] [[thm-circle-integrals-of-integer-monomials]] and [[thm-cauchy-integral-formula-circle]] provide the scalar circle kernel integrals, extended to operator-valued integrals by testing continuous scalar pairings and uniform norm limits. [[thm-dominated-convergence]] applies to the bounded scalar spectral integrals. The annular contour independence and Riesz projection identities required here are derived explicitly below; a self-adjoint PVM for complex $H_\lambda$ is not presumed.

proof_used_steps.claim: [Idempotence without a complex PVM] For each fixed $\lambda$, the inverse norm bound in step 2.1 and another Neumann series give an open annulus around $\Gamma$ consisting of resolvent points. Within this annulus, circle integrals of a holomorphic operator function are independent of radius: differentiating $\int_0^{2\pi}f(E+re^{it})ire^{it}dt$ in $r$ gives the integral of the $t$ derivative of $f(E+re^{it})e^{it}$, which is zero by periodicity. Choose concentric outer and inner circles in the annulus. The inverse equations give $R_\lambda(z)R_\lambda(w)=[R_\lambda(w)-R_\lambda(z)]/(z-w)$ on the two circles. In the double integral of this identity, integrating the first term in the outer variable gives its inner projection integral because $\oint dz/(z-w)=2\pi i$; integrating the second term in the inner variable gives zero because $\oint dw/(z-w)=0$. Interchanging continuous compact integrals is justified by norm Riemann sums. Both circle projections equal $P_\lambda$ by annular independence, so $P_\lambda^2=P_\lambda$. Resolvents commute by the same identity, and thus commute with $P_\lambda$. Also $H_\lambda R_\lambda(z)=zR_\lambda(z)-I$. Integrating in the graph norm of the closed $H_\lambda$ shows $P_\lambda H\subseteq D(H_0)$ and $H_\lambda P_\lambda=(2\pi i)^{-1}\oint zR_\lambda(z)dz$, a bounded operator; the inverse equations on $D(H_0)$ give $P_\lambda H_\lambda=H_\lambda P_\lambda$ there. The uniform series makes $P_\lambda$ and this bounded $H_\lambda P_\lambda$ holomorphic in $\lambda$.

[The initial projection and full-disk rank argument] At $\lambda=0$, [F1] evaluates the scalar contour integrals against the spectral measures of $H_0$: their support misses the circle, and the circle integral of $(z-t)^{-1}$ is one for $|t-E|<g/2$ and zero outside. Hence $P_{\lambda=0}=E_{H_0}(\{E\})=P_0$. The circle length is $\pi g$, so the difference estimate in step 2.1 gives $\|P_\lambda-P_0\|\le q/(1-q)$. For bounded idempotents $P,Q$ with $\|P-Q\|<1$, $Qx=0$, $x\in\operatorname{ran}P$, implies $\|x\|=\|(P-Q)x\|<\|x\|$ unless $x=0$. Thus $Q|_{\operatorname{ran}P}$ is injective, and the reverse restriction is injective by the same argument. For fixed $\lambda$ and $s,t\in[0,1]$, the inverse equations give $R_{s\lambda}(z)-R_{t\lambda}(z)=(s-t)\lambda R_{s\lambda}(z)VR_{t\lambda}(z)$, so $\|P_{s\lambda}-P_{t\lambda}\|\le q|s-t|/(1-q)^2$. Choose an integer $N>q/(1-q)^2$ and compare the finite sequence $P_{j\lambda/N}$, $0\le j\le N$. Consecutive distances are less than one, so the two injections preserve the one-dimensional rank at every step. Therefore $P_\lambda$ has rank one for every $q<1$, even when its distance from $P_0$ is not less than one.

[The entire interior spectrum is one simple eigenvalue] The invariant one-dimensional range of $P_\lambda$ supports a scalar $E_\lambda$ with $H_\lambda P_\lambda=E_\lambda P_\lambda$. Since $R_\lambda(z)P_\lambda=(z-E_\lambda)^{-1}P_\lambda$, the projection integral and $P_\lambda\ne0$ imply that $E_\lambda$ lies strictly inside the circle. For any $w$ inside it define the bounded operator $B(w)=(2\pi i)^{-1}\oint R_\lambda(z)/(z-w)dz$. Its range lies in $D(H_0)$ by graph-norm integration, and the inverse equations give $(w-H_\lambda)B(w)=I-P_\lambda$ on $H$ and $B(w)(w-H_\lambda)=I-P_\lambda$ on $D(H_0)$. It commutes with $P_\lambda$. Its product with $P_\lambda$ is zero: the scalar integral of $[(z-E_\lambda)(z-w)]^{-1}$ is zero, both when the two interior poles are distinct by partial fractions and when equal by the double-pole monomial integral. Thus $B(w)$ is the two-sided inverse of $w-H_\lambda$ on $\ker P_\lambda$, including the exact restricted domain. For $w\ne E_\lambda$, $B(w)+(w-E_\lambda)^{-1}P_\lambda$ is the two-sided inverse on all $H$, proving absence of any other interior spectrum. At $w=E_\lambda$, the complementary inverse excludes complementary eigenvectors and generalized eigenvectors, while the rank-one range has no nontrivial Jordan chain. The eigenspace and algebraic multiplicity are therefore precisely those asserted in (b).

[Holomorphic eigenvalue and the real-coupling interpretation] Around any coupling $\lambda_0$ choose a nonzero $x\in\operatorname{ran}P_{\lambda_0}$ and the continuous complex-linear functional $\ell(y)=\langle y,x\rangle$. Continuity makes $\ell(P_\lambda x)\ne0$ nearby. There $E_\lambda=\ell(H_\lambda P_\lambda x)/\ell(P_\lambda x)$ is holomorphic by step 3.1. The uniqueness of step 5.1 makes these locally defined functions agree, so $E_\lambda$ is holomorphic throughout the disk. For real $\lambda$, self-adjointness from step 2.1 and [F1] imply $E_\lambda\in\mathbb R$; the same scalar contour evaluation as in step 4.1, now applied to $H_\lambda$, identifies $P_\lambda$ with its orthogonal PVM projection on the interior, hence on $\{E_\lambda\}$. For complex coupling the valid construction is the Riesz projection of steps 3.1–5.1. All claims follow on arbitrary $H$ under CC without adding separability or AC.
